newsitem.title: RWANDA: More Rwanda refugees join East Zaire exodus.
newsitem.headline: More Rwanda refugees join East Zaire exodus.

text.p: A week-long exodus of Rwandan Hutu refugees from eastern Zaire continued unabated on Monday with at least 1,000 more people crossing, aid officials said.

Most crossing into Rwanda at Gisenyi's Petite Barriere border point, site of a mass influx of around 500,000 Rwandan Hutus last week, described a harrowing walk through forests and foothills of Masisi district after fleeing Kitale camp south of Goma.
But tired and hungry, none said they had met either the Hutu Interahamwe militia and their former Rwandan army allies or Zairean rebels whose siege of the camps led to the exodus.

"We were dying of thirst, but thank God the rain came," said Drocella Kayisire, a mother of three from Gisenyi. "But the problem in the forest is hunger. People are exhausted and have no strength left."
Aid officials said two days of heavy rain would be a lifesaver to thousands of refugees they believe are stranded in eastern Zaire.
Many reported being robbed by gangs of Zaireans as they passed small villages in the hills and they said tens of thousands of fellow refugees were trapped in the forest behind them, too weak to walk.
Meanwhile authorities in Gisenyi were preparing to clear a transit camp containing over 3,000 former local people that has mushroomed in the past week.
Residents said officials told them they would have to return to their former homes on Tuesday. If the homes were occupied or destroyed, they said, they had been told to camp next door.

Rehousing those who have have returned since fleeing aftermath of the 1994 slaughter in which up to one million Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed is seen as one of the biggest hurdles facing Rwanda as it attempts to rebuild.

As the Tutsi-led Rwandan Patriotic Front routed the Interahamwe and former Rwandan army to crush the genocide, hundreds of thousands of Hutus fled to neighbouring Zaire and Tanzania to escape possible reprisals.
Over 500,000 of them have now returned -- many to find their homes occupied by Tutsis or simply destroyed. Their lands lie fallow or have been planted by farmers who took over abandoned fields.

But for many in Gisenyi, their homes were taken over by relations who stayed behind. "I went to my house and saw my cousin there," said one refugee at the temporary camp. "I stayed there for one night and tomorrow I will go back. They will make room for us."
